Earnings season is in full swing, and Big Tech calls are about more than the heavy use of "superintelligence," which some read as a bid to please the White House after it reportedly disliked the term "artificial intelligence."
Here are three moments from the earnings calls of Tesla (TSLA), Meta (META), and IBM (IBM) on late Wednesday that stuck with us.
Tesla
Much of the focus today is on Tesla cutting its capital spending plans for this year to $20 billion from the $25 billion it guided to three months ago. A key factor appears to be that its Optimus robots need more training before they're released into the real world.
Elon Musk said investors should think of Optimus as a baby:
"A big difference with Optimus versus the cars is we don't have this vast fleet of cars from which we can gather training data. With Optimus, we have to bootstrap it by making the robots and having them do self-play, which is really how a human learns to navigate the world. You can see this when you have a toddler, and they grow up, and initially, they're sort of wobbly, and they don't know how to do things. Eventually they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone. As anyone who's had kids knows. Then they learn to read and do all sorts of things and be able to do these things. They learn this by playing. We actually need Optimus to play at scale in order to have it be really good at tasks in the real world."
Meta
Are early users of Meta's (META) Muse AI agent overspending? Mark Zuckerberg's comments on credit limits during the earnings call suggest they might be.
That raises a bigger question: Could AI agent shopping end badly for retailers and banks, in the form of unpaid debts and write-offs?
"The most common use case for Muse is shopping, with more than a quarter of people who are using Muse engaging in this with an average purchase size of over $200," Zuckerberg said on the call. "Plaid told us that they hadn't seen activity like they're seeing with their connector on any other service before. In the first week, we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected."
IBM
IBM (IBM) CEO Arvind Krishna seemed to be in a better place this earnings call compared to three months ago, which came on the heels of a shock earnings warning that sent the stock reeling.
It was interesting to hear Krishna call out some C-suite concerns about the current spending on AI tools:
"I think what we are seeing is that at least larger enterprises are becoming a lot more cognizant and a lot more aware of what is the true ROI of all of their AI spend. They are also getting worried if some of the AI spending completely out of control with no real return. But the way I have always characterized it is, there is no question to us, and this is the advice I give every C-suite member that I meet, that what we are trying to give people on AI, the productivity, the advantages of AI, the way it is going to change work, is very real. Let me not make any confusion around that."

Hedge Funds Are Ramping Up Stock Shorts to Five-Year Highs. Goldman is Warning of a Squeeze.
Short sales have outpaced long purchases across global equities by about five to one this month.
Hedge funds are building bets against stocks to unusually elevated levels, creating conditions that could turn a market rebound into a sharp rally as bearish investors scramble to unwind their positions.
Bloomberg reported Thursday that hedge funds' bearish stock exposure was approaching a five-year high, citing Goldman Sachs data. The buildup raises the risk of a short squeeze, in which rising prices pressure short sellers to buy back shares, potentially accelerating the advance.
Short sales have outpaced long purchases across global equities by about five to one this month. Short leverage in Goldman's prime brokerage book stood at the 99th percentile of its five-year history, indicating bearish exposure was higher than in almost all of that period.
The figures reveal a market increasingly positioned for weakness and expose a vulnerability. Investors seeking protection against falling prices can become buyers if markets move against them.
Goldman's data showed net leverage among fundamental long-short funds near a three-year low, even as gross leverage increased. Net leverage measures the difference between long and short exposure, while gross leverage combines both. The combination suggests reduced directional exposure without a corresponding retreat from overall trading commitments.
The defensive positioning follows weeks of pressure on hedge funds, particularly those exposed to artificial intelligence stocks. Global fundamental long-short funds lost 2.9% in the week through October 15, suffering losses every trading day during that stretch. Asia-focused stock pickers were down 6.8% for the first half of October, according to Goldman.
Goldman had already highlighted unusually cautious positioning earlier this month. In an interview, Mark Wilson, the bank's head of European Equity Franchise Sales and Hedge Fund Coverage, described hedge funds' net equity exposure as historically low amid volatility in interest rates and energy prices. He said higher yields and other uncertainties had prompted investors to reassess their equity risk.
Those concerns help explain demand for protection. Higher borrowing costs can weigh on stock valuations, while energy price increases can threaten corporate margins and complicate the inflation outlook. Wilson pointed to both forces in discussing the market's recent adjustment.
Short selling typically involves borrowing shares and selling them, with the intention of repurchasing them at a lower price. The difference, after costs, becomes the seller's profit. If shares rise instead, buying them back becomes more expensive. The Securities and Exchange Commission notes that potential losses are theoretically unlimited because a stock's price has no fixed ceiling.
A price increase forces some short sellers to cover; their purchases lift prices further, and additional investors face pressure to close their trades. Heavy short exposure does not establish when a rally will begin, and short positions can also serve as hedges against stocks a fund owns.

In July, IBM (IBM +0.26%) stock suffered the worst day in its 115-year history, falling about 25% after the company warned that customers had shifted spending away from its products.
The miss was clearly a matter of timing -- a series of major contracts IBM was planning didn't close by the end of the quarter, as its customers shifted spending to memory and storage products whose prices were increasing rapidly.
Three months later, IBM's third-quarter report, which landed on Oct. 21, mostly backed that assessment up, and the company posted strong revenue and earnings. So, why isn't the stock bouncing back?
Image source: Getty Images.
The good news was real
IBM's revenue rose 5% to $17.1 billion in the third quarter, up from 1% growth in the second. Software grew 9% at constant currency, and operating earnings per share rose 11% to $2.95. Free cash flow was $3 billion, and management raised its full-year outlook to FCF growth of more than $1 billion.
CFO Jim Kavanaugh said about two-thirds of the large software deals that slipped in the second quarter closed in the third. Transaction processing software, which is tied to mainframes, swung from a 9% decline to 10% growth. That looks like delayed spending, not lost customers.

Some of that growth was bought
IBM closed its roughly $11 billion acquisition of Confluent in March, so that revenue wasn't included in last year's numbers. Confluent's last reported quarterly revenue was $314.8 million, and IBM's software revenue in Q3 2025 was $7.2 billion. So that would put IBM's organic software growth in this quarter at around 4%. That's real progress, but it's less dramatic than 9%.
Management is also tapping the brakes. CEO Arvind Krishna said he doesn't expect transaction processing to keep growing at double digits, and IBM expects that business to be flat for the year. Kavanaugh said the company is expecting about $32 billion in full-year software revenue. Subtract the $22.6 billion IBM has recognized through nine months, and the fourth quarter works out to roughly 4% growth, versus 8% in the third. Mainframe hardware sales also fell 20%, although that came against a very strong launch a year ago.
IBM is a long-term buy
I still like IBM as a long-term investment in AI and quantum computing, but I'm not ignoring the risks. IBM spent $11.4 billion on acquisitions this year, so cash fell $3.4 billion to $11.1 billion, and debt rose $2.6 billion to $63.8 billion. The dividend looks well covered -- IBM paid $4.8 billion of dividends against $7.8 billion of free cash flow through nine months -- but there's less cushion for another big deal. Meanwhile, shareholders receive a dividend yield of about 2.7%.

The company has established itself as an important player in enterprise AI, while its hybrid cloud business and consulting operations provide opportunities for long-term growth.
There are challenges, particularly as businesses remain cautious about technology spending. But IBM has something many high-flying AI stocks don't -- an established customer base, consistent cash flow, and a reliable dividend.

Alphabet's (GOOG -3.08%) (GOOGL -3.15%) Google is one of the world's largest cloud infrastructure companies, yet it just started paying SpaceX (SPCX -9.14%) $920 million per month -- or $11 billion per year -- to lease xAI's cloud infrastructure through 2029. Let's see why Google is renting that cloud compute from SpaceX rather than building more data centers -- and how that unusual deal could expose it to some unpredictable concentration risks in the future.
Why does Google need SpaceX's data centers?
Google controlled 15% of the global cloud infrastructure market in the second quarter of 2026, according to Synergy Research Group, putting it in third place after Amazon (AMZN -4.57%) Web Services (AWS) (28%) and Microsoft (MSFT -2.23%) Azure (20%).
From 2021 to 2025, Google Cloud's annual revenue more than tripled from $19.2 billion to $58.7 billion as the cloud and AI markets expanded, and Google seems like a great vertically integrated play on those secular trends. The tech titan builds its own data centers, produces its own custom AI chips, and hosts a broad range of market-leading cloud-based services and apps. It also ties all of those pieces together with Gemini and its other AI models.
But over the past few years, Google couldn't expand that infrastructure fast enough to keep pace with the AI market's explosive growth. It produced enough of its custom tensor processing units (TPUs) for its own first-party cloud services, but most of its customers needed access to Nvidia's (NVDA -4.40%) graphics processing units (GPUs), which are better suited for training other AI models. Most of the top AI companies -- including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta Platforms -- use Nvidia's data center GPUs to process their AI tasks.
Nvidia controls over 80% of the data center AI chip market, and it locks in those customers with its proprietary software and services. A large portion of Google's servers already run on Nvidia's GPUs, but it doesn't have nearly enough chips to satisfy the market's demand for Nvidia-powered cloud computing services. To fill that gap, Google is willing to pay SpaceX $11 billion per year for continuous access to a cluster of roughly 110,000 GPUs.

Is that a smart long-term decision?

However, it would also have had to secure enough power to run those GPUs -- and it can take three to five years to set up new grid connections for data centers. Google would also need to pay massive energy and labor expenses to continuously operate those centers, and the value of its existing GPUs would depreciate as soon as Nvidia launches newer chips.
Moreover, it could take a long time for Nvidia -- which is still selling chips faster than it can produce them -- to actually fulfill that massive order. Instead of dealing with all of that, it makes more sense for Google to just pay $11 billion (less than 2% of its projected 2027 revenue) to instantly increase its cloud computing power and keep pace with Amazon and Microsoft. “The best ideas have a shelf life,” Stokes said, arguing that marketers need the ability to act while a customer moment is still occurring.

According to recent report from AM Best, commercial auto liability insurance coverage has continued to bear the brunt of rising litigation costs, outpacing economic inflation.
Social inflation has negatively affected commercial auto liability ultimate claim costs for several years, which is evident by looking at average claim severity. Economic inflation from 2014 to 2024 averaged 2.8% annually. Over the same period, commercial auto liability insurance loss payments for the first 12 months have trended upward at 6.4% annually—more than double the annual increase of economic inflation, AM Best said.
AM Best defines social inflation as the rising cost of insurance claims that exceeds general economic inflation, driven by societal and legal trends like higher jury awards, increased litigation, and expanded definitions of liability.
AM Best Special Report: Social Inflation Adds Pressure to US Property/Casualty Liability Results
Commercial auto liability losses are capped by policy limits, typically $1 million. Individual auto claims resulting in loss payments exceeding that threshold will fall to an umbrella policy if that type of coverage is in place.
Through 2018, umbrella pricing tracked closely with general liability pricing. However, as social inflation began to impact commercial auto claims, and those claims spilled into umbrella coverages, the pricing on the latter has diverged from general liability, becoming more costly, and has yet to return to its prior level.
Historically, umbrella pricing followed closely with general liability but more recently, David Blades, associate director at AM Best said, “As social inflation began to impact commercial auto claims, and those claims spilled into the umbrella coverage, umbrella pricing diverged from general liability, becoming more costly.”
Among the report’s other highlights:
- Claims being open longer leaves more exposure to jury precedent, in addition to most likely resulting in elevated claim adjustment expenses.
- After adjusting for settlement rates, commercial auto claim frequency has increased over the past 10 years, which also creates a gap in what has been paid and what is expected to be paid.
- Tort reforms may help. Sweeping tort reforms in Florida have helped offset excessive litigation costs, resulting in average paid claim severity to trend downward.

Having spent more than 20 years in the industry, including a decade focusing on builder’s risk, I have seen the market shift numerous times over the years.
In my opinion, here’s what lies behind the three biggest factors currently influencing Builder’s Risk:
Project stagnation
The number of submissions for Builder’s Risk are up compared to recent years, but the time from quote to bind is considerably longer. In DUAL’s experience, a project used to take 90 days to bind and that has now stretched out substantially further.
Uncertainty is at the heart of stagnation. Tariffs and other geopolitical factors are disrupting supply chains from China and the Strait of Hormuz as well as increasing costs of materials across the builders’ risk space. For example, lumber is typically sourced from Canada and tariffs have increased prices by roughly half prompting builders to delay project starts in hopes these tariffs will ease. Other issues are more item specific. The global rush to construct data centers has added to the power demand which has resulted in a five-year lead time for combined cycle turbines, meaning any contingent BI loss tied to that delay could be potentially catastrophic.
‘Spicy’ loss ratios
Despite being in a soft market, loss ratios are still running high. Builder’s Risk claims always occur many months after policy inception and project delays are stretching timelines out even further. Underwriters need to remain disciplined and recognize the loss ratio impacts of today’s decisions may not impact carriers for a couple of years. Brokers have an important role in keeping underwriters apprised with up-to-date information regarding what they are seeing from clients and the building market in general.
Arson remains a significant loss contributor with many claims stemming from ‘not-in-my-backyard’ arson-related incidents. Recently, Salt Lake City UT and Aurora CO have seen a spate of arson attacks on developments. Several carriers have also cut their security requirements due to the soft market, and this could lead to future higher loss ratios.
Generational change
It is great to see large numbers of younger insurance professionals, both brokers and underwriters, choosing to specialize in the niche. The generational shift and current market conditions are spurring increased creativity. There is more ‘out-of-the-box’ thinking across all disciplines, including some clever use of AI.
People new to the sector should be aware that the current surplus of capacity is not likely to last, and it is important to build strong, stable partnerships with carriers for the long term. This has always been a key focus at DUAL.
How people are building relationships across the industry is changing too. Creativity and innovation has focused on unique activities such as cooking classes, yoga sessions, and using AI to help plan different activities. While the activities may be changing, fundamentally, underwriting remains a people business. One focused on connection which builds trust through the underwriting cycle that creates good outcomes for the client, broker and underwriter.
Like all insurance products, the market runs in cycles. Being aware and on top of the drivers of each current cycle and understanding how the market has reacted to these drivers historically , improves decision making going forward.

US equity markets typically rise following midterm elections, but many on Wall Street aren't convinced the outcome matters as much as long-term fundamentals do.

The S&P 500 has posted an average gain of about 15% in the 12 months following midterm elections since 1950, J.P. Morgan Asset Management said in a note Oct. 7.
That's because getting past elections helps markets refocus on the fundamentals that include corporate earnings, monetary policy and the artificial intelligence spending boom, J.P. Morgan Global Market Strategist Jordan Jackson said.
"In short, history is on the side of investors after midterms," Jackson said. "Rather than trying to trade around the election, investors should stay invested, remain diversified and keep their focus on the longer-term drivers of returns."

"No statistic should be taken in isolation," Jackson said. "Past midterm cycles have unfolded against very different economic backdrops."

Before International Business Machines (IBM +0.26%) posted third-quarter results on Oct. 21, I set a bar for buying the stock. I wanted software revenue growth back in the high single digits and recurring revenue rising close to 10%.
The software half of that test came through. IBM's software segment reported 9% year-over-year revenue growth at constant currency (a measure that strips out exchange-rate moves). In the second quarter, it grew just 5%.
But shares barely budged on Thursday, the day after the report, closing up less than 1% after falling as much as 4% during the session. IBM stock closed at $252.11, which puts it about 23% under the $329.23 record close it set on June 2.
In September, I wrote that I expected IBM stock to be higher in five years but still wouldn't buy it. What I was waiting for was software growth that picked back up. I think this quarter delivered it.

Software is growing faster again
Software matters more to IBM's profits than any other piece of the business. The segment made up around 46% of third-quarter revenue but about 65% of the company's segment profit, so its swing this year counts for a lot.
Software's constant-currency growth was 8% in the first quarter of 2026. It cooled to 5% in the second quarter before jumping to 9% in the third -- its fastest rate of the year. Transaction processing, the software linked largely to IBM's mainframes, did most of the swinging. It dropped 9% at constant currency in the second quarter and climbed 10% in the third. Better still, software's segment profit rose 15% year over year to around $2.7 billion, and its margin widened to 35% from 33%.
"Software revenue growth accelerated four points sequentially to 9% this quarter, including over four points of organic growth," chief financial officer Jim Kavanaugh said on IBM's Oct. 21 earnings call.
Granted, some of the jump is timing. Kavanaugh said around a quarter of the acceleration came from big deals that slipped out of the second quarter and closed in the third. The other three-quarters, he said, came from new business.
I think this makes the second quarter look like the exception, not the start of a slide.
Does the unchanged revenue forecast matter?
IBM still expects full-year revenue to climb 4% to 5% at constant currency, the same range it set in July. But it now expects 2026 free cash flow to rise by over $1 billion from last year's $14.7 billion. In July, it expected a gain of around $1 billion.
Kavanaugh said IBM ties its profit and cash flow plans to a 4% base case for revenue, and it kept that approach this quarter. Under that plan, IBM now expects software to grow about 7% to 8% this year, with 7% as the base case.
I don't think the unchanged revenue forecast takes much away from the software turn. Software carries most of IBM's profit, so a faster software business can raise cash flow even when total revenue growth stays in the same range. And third-quarter free cash flow climbed around 28% year over year to $3.0 billion.
Recurring revenue is the half of my test that hasn't shown up yet. IBM's annual recurring revenue, a yearly run-rate measure of its recurring software business, grew 8% to $24.9 billion, still below 10%. But Kavanaugh said he expects that growth to near double digits in the fourth quarter.

Russia-linked hackers used the volunteer-run Yggdrasil network to conceal communications during an attack on a Ukrainian grain logistics company, marking the first documented use of the technology by a state-linked hacking group, cybersecurity firm ESET said on Thursday.
The attack culminated in the destruction of data at the company, which forms part of Ukraine’s vital agricultural export sector. Agriculture accounted for roughly a fifth of Ukraine’s economy and nearly half its exports before the war, according to research estimates.
ESET traced the July 2025 intrusion to a phishing email sent as part of an ongoing campaign targeting logistics firms, grain companies and port terminals in Ukraine, researcher Anton Cherepanov said.
The attackers installed software that allowed them to remotely control infected computers, browse files, take screenshots and steal documents. The software communicated through a server hidden inside Yggdrasil, an experimental volunteer-run network with no central owner.
“Because it’s a mesh network, it’s harder to detect,” Cherepanov said. ESET said it had not previously observed state-linked attacks using the network.
After gaining administrator privileges, the attackers activated a data-wiping tool that deleted data from affected computers, Cherepanov said. The tool used was SDelete, a legitimate Microsoft utility designed to permanently erase files.
“They abused this legitimate tool,” he said.
“SDelete is a legitimate, publicly available administrative utility that IT professionals use to securely delete data. Like many legitimate tools, it can be misused by malicious actors who have already gained access to a network,” a Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters in an email.
ESET said it could not determine what the affected systems were used for and could not confirm whether the attack disrupted grain operations.
The initial intrusion was carried out by a Russia-linked hacking group known as UAC-0099, which ESET said specializes in gaining access to networks. The subsequent data destruction bore the hallmarks of Sandworm, a hacking group widely linked to Russian military intelligence and previously blamed for cyberattacks on Ukrainian and Polish power infrastructure.
ESET assessed that UAC-0099 successfully gained access and handed it to Sandworm, but said it could not determine which group operated the previously unseen backdoor used between the breach and the data destruction.
The firm declined to identify the victim company.

Storm Austen knocked out electricity to almost 300,000 customers in western France on Friday as hurricane-force winds battered the region, disrupting roads, railways and other transport links.
Brittany was hardest hit, with almost 150,000 customers without power, according to distributor Enedis. Amber weather alerts are in place across northwest Spain and France, and the western half of Germany. One region in northern Germany near the Harz Mountains is under a red alert for high winds.
Airports on Jersey and Guernsey were closed. Cancellations and delays are mounting at Paris airports, according to data from Flight tracking site Flightradar24.
Read more: Storm Austen Will Be Stronger Than Forecast Along UK Coasts
Austen is the first named storm this autumn and it’s also sending power prices in France and Germany tumbling. A surge in wind generation is flooding grids with cheap electricity, offering some relief to markets that have been grappling with the highest natural gas prices since the 2022 energy crisis.
In Germany, Europe’s biggest power market, wind generation is poised to set a new output record on Friday and could come close to meeting all the nation’s needs on Sunday, although curtailment and must-run generation may limit actual output. Kpler SA forecasts that power prices will drop to €29 a megawatt-hour on Saturday and near zero on Sunday, the lowest since April.
French prices are also forecast to plunge, falling to about €17 on Sunday, the lowest since June. The burst of wind generation reduces the need for more expensive gas-fired plants, which often set prices when renewable output is low.
Austen swept through the English Channel on Friday, lashing both coasts of France and England with heavy rain. Gusts as high as 140 kilometers per hour (87 miles) are expected in some French coastal areas, equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale, according to Météo-France.
Enedis has mobilized more than 2,000 personnel since Wednesday, with several hundred additional technicians being sent to the hardest-hit areas as part of its rapid response force. In Normandy, cuts affected 88,800 customers, 49,600 in Pays de la Loire and almost 8,000 in Hauts-de-France, Enedis said.
The storm also disrupted transport across northern and western France. Several roads and train lines around Paris and in Normandy, Brittany and Hauts-de-France were interrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said on X.
In the UK, airports on the Channel Islands of Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney were closed until Friday afternoon. About 20,000 people lost power in southwest England, according to National Grid.
The UK day-ahead power price for Saturday settled at £37 per megawatt-hour, less than half of the average so far this year according to data from Epex Spot.
A second storm, named Boelo, is set to follow this weekend, taking a more northerly route across Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England, according to the UK Met Office. Boelo could bring winds of as much as 129 kilometers an hour to coastal areas along with heavy rain. The UK has issued amber weather warnings for that storm starting Saturday.
The storm patterns could push wind speeds in Europe’s key power markets to 31% above the 10-year average through Nov. 4, helping to offset increased heating demand and weaker solar generation, BloombergNEF said in a note.

New York’s City Council voted to ban horse-drawn carriages, ending a Central Park tourist staple dating to the 19th century after years of debate over the horses’ place on city streets.
The Council voted 40 to 7 to pass the bill Thursday, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani is expected to sign. Two members abstained. The ban takes effect June 1, 2028, and prohibits the sale of horses for slaughter or their transfer to other carriage companies.
The vote ends a fight that has simmered for more than a decade, pitting the city’s roughly 150 carriage drivers and their union against animal-rights advocates and drawing in politicians and celebrities on both sides. Supporters see the clip-clop of hooves through Central Park as part of New York’s appeal, romanticized in film and television; critics say horse-drawn carriages are an anachronism ill-suited to the city’s traffic, pollution and crowded streets.
As the council prepared to vote, President Donald Trump weighed in, criticizing the city’s lawmakers.
“The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience,” Trump, who was born in New York, wrote in a social media post. “So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!”
The legislation includes a promise to construct a plan by April 1, 2027, for aiding carriage drivers in finding new jobs after the ban takes effect. That plan could include financial compensation for carriage drivers and owners, but doesn’t guarantee it.
Sixty-eight horse cabs are currently licensed to operate in Central Park, under a system that’s capped the number of carriages since the second World War. In addition to the drivers, the industry has more than 180 horses, according to industry spokesperson Christina Hansen.
Carriage industry employees and horse and stable owners say the bill doesn’t go far enough in providing for their financial futures.
“This bill is a train wreck of constitutional and due process violations,” John Samuelsen, president of the Transport Workers Union International, which represents the carriage drivers, said in a statement. “It offers nothing concrete for blue-collar drivers and carriage owners who will be financially crushed, stripped of their jobs, their licenses, expensive city-issued medallions, small businesses, and way of life.”
The union has vowed to seek a temporary restraining order after Mamdani signs the bill.
“We will see them in court,” said Alexander Kemp, administrative vice president for a New York chapter of the union. “This fight is not over.”
The carriages have long faced opposition from animal rights activists who argue that forcing the horses to work in urban conditions damages their long-term health and is unsafe.

Taiwan shut its $5 trillion stock market, schools and offices on Friday as Typhoon Champi barreled toward the island, bringing heavy rain and damaging winds that disrupted flights.
Champi was packing top sustained winds of 155 kilometers (96 miles) an hour, equivalent to a Category 2 hurricane, according to the island’s weather agency, after weakening over the past 24 hours from super typhoon strength. The storm was around 260 kilometers southeast of Taipei’s Taoyuan International Airport as of 2:30 p.m. Friday local time, the bureau added.
Most of Taiwan’s cities and counties shut offices and schools for safety on Friday, while the storm had already killed one person and injured 171, according to government statements. More than 950 international and domestic flights were canceled on Friday, along with some train services.
Read more: Taiwan Halts Stock Trade, Shuts Schools as Typhoon Champi Nears
Taiwan’s stock exchange, the fifth-largest globally, will also be closed Monday for a holiday, giving the island an additional trading gap compared with other markets in the region. The tech-heavy exchange, along with those in South Korea and Japan, has sold off recently as investors track earnings from global tech giants.
Cooler ocean waters and increasing wind shear will steadily shave some intensity from Champi, but it remains a very large cyclone with an expansive wind field, according to the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center. The storm is forecast to pass just east of Taipei early Saturday before curving northeast along mainland China’s east coast on its way toward Japan’s Kyushu.
“The risks that matter now are rain and the size of the wind field,” said James Caron, director of meteorological operations for North America and Asia at Atmospheric G2. “The 185-miles-per-hour peak is behind us.”
Champi achieved super typhoon strength earlier in the week, making it the 10th to reach that level in the northwest Pacific Ocean this season. That’s double the long-term average and just shy of a record 13 during 2015’s El Niño, according to the Hong Kong Observatory. Storms tend to form farther east during the climate phenomenon, giving them more time to accumulate energy over warm, open waters as they churn toward land.

E-bikes now rival motorcycles for speed. State and city laws haven’t caught up.
Electric bikes and electric scooters parked on a street in Columbus, Ohio. Lawmakers in Ohio and many other states have enacted or are considering tougher regulations for e-bikes and e-scooters as their popularity – and safety concerns – grow. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal).
Earlier this month, a 50-year-old man riding his personal electric scooter in Washington, D.C., was killed when he collided with a woman on a rideshare scooter.
In June, a 12-year-old Massachusetts girl died after her electric scooter slammed into a school bus in a suburb of Boston.
And in April, an Atlanta woman riding an electric bike was killed when she hit a curb and was thrown headfirst into a wall.
A string of high-profile deaths and injuries involving electric scooters and bikes is spurring states and cities across the country to crack down on them. As technology improves, e-scooters and e-bikes capable of motorcycle-like speeds have become cheaper and more popular. Some models — and the ability to modify them with aftermarket upgrades — are blurring the lines between bicycles, scooters and motor vehicles.
State and local regulations, many of which were originally written to manage the glut of low-speed rideshare scooters nearly a decade ago, haven’t kept pace, some experts say, and they’ve left city officials scrambling to do more.
The victim in the Washington, D.C., incident was Talib Shakir, who worked in the office of D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser. Police said neither Shakir nor the woman he collided with was wearing a helmet, and that Shakir’s e-scooter could reach speeds up to 55 miles per hour.
A few days later, D.C.’s Metropolitan Police launched a street safety initiative focused on educating e-bike and e-scooter riders about road safety.
In New York City, local leaders held a hearing in August to discuss a slate of new regulations for e-bikes and e-scooters. As of September, at least 28 New Yorkers riding electric devices have died in crashes, the city’s highest-ever total by that point in the year.
A month before the Massachusetts accident, Gov. Maura Healey proposed legislation to establish safety standards and other regulations for e-scooters and e-bikes.
Healey, a Democrat, called existing laws around so-called micromobility devices “unclear and inconsistent,” in a May 2026 statement announcing her bill, which is currently in committee.
“We are seeing too much reckless behavior, more crashes and close calls,” she said, “and too many people, especially pedestrians and young riders, are at risk.”
And after several highly publicized deaths in the Atlanta metro area, including the woman who died after she was thrown from her bike and a teen who died when his e-scooter collided with a tractor-trailer, local officials in surrounding communities have been under pressure to address safety issues.
States including Illinois, Michigan and Pennsylvania have enacted or considered new restrictions this year. Cost of employer-sponsored health insurance plans rises again, nonpartisan survey finds
The price health insurance companies charge for employer-sponsored plans increased again this year, according to a survey by KFF (krisanapong detraphiphat/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — The price health insurance companies charge for employer-sponsored plans increased again this year, as did the deductible many people must pay before those plans begin covering most healthcare costs, according to a survey released Thursday by the nonpartisan health organization KFF.
The cost of individual health insurance plans rose to $9,804 on average, while family coverage reached $28,303. Both represented a 5% increase over the last year.
Employees paid about $1,672 for individual coverage, while employers contributed $8,132. People with health insurance for a family of four paid $7,471, with employers providing $20,833.
The amount of money an employee pays toward an individual health insurance plan rose by $232, or 16%, from 2025 to 2026. The price an employee pays for a family health insurance policy increased by $621, or 9%, according to the survey.
“We have been hearing a lot about Affordable Care Act and Medicaid cuts,” KFF President and CEO Drew Altman said in a statement. “Now add a 9% increase in what workers with employer coverage paid toward family premiums in 2026 to the reasons voters are so concerned about their health care costs.”
The national survey looked at the health insurance costs of more than 1,900 employers throughout the country who have at least 10 workers.
The cost of employer-sponsored health insurance plans has steadily gone up for the last 15 years, according to KFF’s data. In 2011, the cost of an individual plan totaled just under $5,500 and family plans cost $15,220 annually.
The average deductible reached $1,995 for single coverage this year, meaning even with health insurance, most employees had to pay a couple thousand dollars out of pocket before their policies kicked in. That’s more than doubled since 2011 when the average annual deductible was $955.
The KFF survey found that 88% of workers with individual coverage had a deductible in 2026.
What types of healthcare coverage people get with the various employer-sponsored health insurance plans varied considerably, sometimes based on the size of their company.
Twenty-seven percent of employers with more than 200 employees, called large firms in the KFF survey, covered the costs of in vitro fertilization, or IVF.
But that fluctuated, with 24% of companies between 200 and 999 workers covering IVF, 38% of companies between 1,000 and 4,999 employees providing coverage and 47% of companies with more than 5,000 workers offering a health insurance plan that covers IVF.

When I was pregnant, my ex-husband pinned me against a wall. I was afraid he would kill me.
I survived that violence. I also have a felony conviction. And those two parts of my life cannot be separated.
My ex-husband and I often used methamphetamine together. Our drug use led to countless arguments, and I endured repeated physical and emotional abuse. When I tried to stay sober, he pressured me to use drugs with him.
Once, while I was sober and he had relapsed, he trapped me in the bedroom of our trailer. For hours, he paced back and forth with a bat, screaming in my face and threatening me.
When someone has that much power over your life, saying no doesn’t always feel safe. At times, I believed my choices were to use drugs or face more violence. I made decisions I regret, but I made them while living in fear.
My methamphetamine use eventually led to my arrest and felony conviction.
I understand that I should be held accountable for the crimes I committed. But accountability and understanding are not mutually exclusive. When the court system ignores the circumstances surrounding a crime, it fails to recognize the full story.
In court, I tried to explain how domestic violence had influenced my decisions. But I felt the judge gave little consideration to what I had endured. I believe that if my abuse had been taken seriously, I might have had a better chance to enter a treatment program, get away from my husband and find sobriety sooner.
Today, I celebrate eight years of sobriety and a home free from abuse. I have earned credentials in addiction counseling and peer support. My life is very different from what it was then, but my conviction remains part of my story.
And my experience is not unique.
Missouri Appleseed, a nonprofit advocating for criminal justice reform, has documented the experiences of women whose abuse and coercion contributed to crimes that led to incarceration.
The organization is championing the Missouri Survivors’ Justice Act, which would give survivors a meaningful opportunity to present evidence of domestic violence or coercion during sentencing.
If abuse contributed to someone’s crime, judges should be required to take those circumstances into account when determining an appropriate sentence.

A class-action lawsuit has been filed in an Australian court against Meta Platforms’ Facebook and Instagram that alleges the social media platforms exposed children to harmful content and kept them addicted through algorithms.
The lawsuit, filed in the Federal Court, Australia’s second-highest, by law firm MinterEllison this month could be the first in Australia to blame social media for harming its users, particularly children and teenagers.
- The class-action suit has been filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs, who allege they were harmed by Meta while they were under the age of 18, and are seeking compensation.
- “We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously,” a Meta spokesperson said by email.
- In a suppression order on Monday, the court prohibited the reporting of any information which could reveal the identity of the applicants, and the statement of claim.
- The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and Big Tech after a world-first ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
- Meta in August agreed to pay $18 billion to settle with nearly all US states to resolve claims it designed social media to addict children.
